 Before his current role, he served as the Washington correspondent (including being the US Bureau Chief for The Sunday Telegraph in the 1990s) and the Europe correspondent (based in Brussels) for The Telegraph. He has also written for The Spectator and The Economist
 Published 
 10 November 2026 2:43pm GMT

 The US economy is overheating. The monetary and fiscal pedals are both pushed to the floor.
 Wage growth is accelerating. Final sales are rising at a 5pc clip. Forward corporate earnings are soaring. The growth rate of nominal GDP is fast approaching 7pc, and heading for 10pc on current policy settings.
 “The AI trade has blown up, but the market has not. None of this is consistent with the idea that the US economy is rolling over,” said Michael Darda, the chief economist at investment bank Roth.
 Jon Hilsenrath, the founder of Serpa Pinto Advisory, said the Federal Reserve over-stimulated with 175 basis points of interest rate cuts in 2024 and 2025. The effects are now feeding through with the time-honoured delay.
 The AI hyperscalers, and the industry of picks and shovels serving them, meet every definition of an unsustainable bubble. But whether this is the big crash we have all been waiting for is another matter. The history of powerful technological booms suggests a torrid rebound before this cycle finally plays out.
 A year ago, I wrote that it was too soon to bail out of Wall Street because the Fed and the US treasury were still pouring rocket fuel on stocks. We are now deeper into late-cycle territory and both institutions are still turbo-charging the economy. The reckoning is pushed further out.
 Giant equity bubbles do not deflate under their own weight. They keep going – longer than we think possible – until the Fed kills them, deliberately or by accident. It was how the electrification and radio boom ended in 1929 and how the telecom and internet boom ended in 2001 (after five rate rises in six months). The subprime boom was different, but ended the same way in 2008 after 13 rate rises in two years.
 The Fed is not doing anything of the sort today under Kevin Warsh, though it will soon have to. The Center for Financial Stability in New York says its measure of broad money – divisia M3 – is picking up speed and growing at 7pc, the fastest pace in almost two decades if you exclude the pandemic.
 Regional Fed presidents are losing patience. Lorrie Logan, the head of the Dallas branch, wants a jumbo rate rise, warning that the Fed is drifting even further away from its inflation target. “We have missed that goal for nearly six years. This is unacceptable.”
 If and when the Fed breaks the fever – that is to say, when inflation forces Warsh to act – the shake-out is going to be painful for the global financial system. It will also be a long-due and deserved comeuppance for an American tech oligarchy that has behaved as badly as the robber barons of the Gilded Age.
 The “Buffett Indicator” measuring the total equity value of the dotcom bubble in the late Nineties – a road map of sorts – peaked at 162pc of GDP. The Trump-Musk-Nvidia bubble is 282pc even after the mini-bloodbath of recent weeks. A serious purge from this level would squeeze spending violently via the wealth effect. It would imply a deep and intractable recession, challenging a US system that has already used up its counter-cyclical fiscal ammo.
 US public debt was 54pc of GDP at the end of the dotcom boom and the federal budget was 2.3pc of GDP in surplus. Today, the debt ratio is 121pc, and heading for 142pc within five years on IMF forecasts. The deficit for this fiscal year was on track for 6.8pc even before the midterm elections.
 Evercore ISI said gridlock could add as much as $320bn (£238bn) of extra spending as each side digs in on its agenda: defence for the Republicans and health care and green tech for the Democrats. “The path of least resistance is likely ‘more for more’,” it said.
 Darda says the hierarchy of AI equity losses so far has been a fall of 31pc for the Generative AI (CHAT) exchange-traded fund, 36pc for the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX), 50pc for neocloud stocks (NCLD) and 51pc for memory chips (DRAM). The Korean Kospi index – a proxy for the AI trade – is down 45pc.
 The AI complex has fallen by roughly the same amount as “tech stocks” did in the first phase of the epic bear markets of 2000 and 1929-1932. Both were followed by a deceptive buy-dip rally regaining half or more of the lost ground before optimists had the stuffing beaten out of them.
 The midterm results tighten the regulatory screws on hyperscalers but do not change the fundamental picture. Growth and earnings forecasts were already make-believe, since the AI industry lacks the electricity infrastructure in the US to meet the voracious demand for compute power.
 Yes, I know, they have marvellous tales about how they will soon be running their data centres on nuclear power from small modular reactors (yet to exist) or, failing that, from refurbished old jet engines plucked out of Boeing’s cemetery in the Mojave Desert.
 Let us be serious. The physical constraint is rock-hard. The US grid has had no major upgrade for half a century and is not fit for purpose. Money alone cannot overcome the global bottleneck of transformers, substations, switchgear and transmission lines.
 Fracking will not help either. The waiting list for heavy-duty gas turbines is five to seven years. Complex metallurgy renders these machines very difficult to make, which is why three companies have locked up the world market.
 Energy supremacy based on fossil fuels alone is proving to be a geriatric delusion. The international economy is moving with irresistible force from molecules to electrons because electrotech is more advanced, better aligned with everything digital, wins on cost and is the only answer to the climate juggernaut bearing down on us … that little matter, so out of political fashion for now.
 We can nearly all agree that AI is for real and will shake the world order to its foundations. But it is a big step to go from there to accept that agentic AI and neocloud companies will ever be able to capture sufficient revenues to validate their share prices or pay their debts, even if hyperscalers may prosper on business software and data analysis.
 Gary Marcus, a professor of neural science at New York University and the scourge of the AI business model, says the industry has no defensive moat. Chinese open-weight rivals are almost as good and will destroy the global pricing power of the US models. “China has all but caught up. Short of government intervention, Anthropic and OpenAI are probably f----d,” he says.
 The clincher for me was learning that Elon Musk’s SpaceX paid $60bn to buy Cursor, a California AI coding company that built its technology on a Chinese foundation model, Kimi 2.5.
 Kevin Warsh’s Federal Reserve held rates in October ahead of the midterm elections, a crucial vote for Donald Trump’s party
 Credit : AP Photo/Alex Brandon
 That said, the market has known about the China threat since the DeepSeek shock in January 2025 and analysts have been fretting for even longer about a “commoditisation” price war. None of this stopped AI equities pushing ever higher.
 Technology revolutions coupled with loose money invariably sweep all before them. It takes iron-fisted policy tightening to rein in the stampede.
 Money is still loose and becoming looser in cyclically adjusted real terms. Warsh has yet to show that he has the mettle to defy his political patron in the White House. I am not selling anything until he does.
